1.1.summary: King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe how the Pandava and Kaurava armies gathered on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

1.2.summary: Sanjaya reports that Duryodhana, after seeing the Pandava army, goes to his teacher Drona and speaks to him.

1.3.summary: Duryodhana addresses Drona, pointing out the impressive Pandava forces arranged by Drupada’s son.

1.4.summary: He lists the heroic warriors on the Pandava side, including great archers and mighty fighters.

1.5.summary: Duryodhana continues naming valiant leaders such as Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, and the king of Kasi among the Pandava allies.

1.6.summary: He mentions the strong Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and the sons of Draupadi as part of the Pandava forces.

1.7.summary: Duryodhana tells Drona to note the most distinguished warriors on his own side, the Kaurava army.

1.8.summary: He lists his own chief fighters: Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava.

1.9.summary: Duryodhana adds that many other heroes are ready to sacrifice their lives for him, all skilled in weapons.

1.10.summary: He claims that his own army, led by Bhishma, is weaker than the Pandava army led by Bhima.

1.11.summary: Duryodhana orders his troops to stay in their positions and protect Bhishma.

1.12.summary: Bhishma, the eldest Kaurava, roars like a lion and blows his conch to encourage Duryodhana.

1.13.summary: Following Bhishma, the Kaurava side sounds conches, drums, and horns, creating a tremendous noise.

1.14.summary: Krishna and Arjuna sit in a splendid chariot drawn by white horses and blow divine conches.

1.15.summary: Krishna blows the Panchajanya conch, Arjuna blows the Devadatta, and Bhima sounds the great conch Paundra.

1.16.summary: Yudhishthira blows the Anantavijaya conch, while Nakula and Sahadeva sound the Sughosha and Manipushpaka.

1.17.summary: The king of Kasi, the archer Sikhandi, the mighty car‑warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki also blow their conches.

1.18.summary: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the son of Subhadra each sound their own conches.

1.19.summary: The thunderous sound of the conches shakes the hearts of Dhritarashtra’s side and makes heaven and earth reverberate.

1.20.summary: Seeing the opposing forces ready for battle, Arjuna takes up his bow and addresses Krishna, the Lord of the earth.

1.21.summary: Arjuna asks Krishna to place his chariot in the middle of the two armies so he can see who is ready to fight.

1.22.summary: Arjuna repeats his request for the chariot to be positioned between the armies to observe the combatants.

1.23.summary: He wants to see the assembled warriors and understand whom he must face to please the hostile Duryodhana.

1.24.summary: Sanjaya reports that Krishna, after Arjuna’s request, positions the chariot in the middle of the two forces for Dhritarashtra to see.

1.25.summary: Krishna points out to Arjuna the assembled Kuru warriors, including Bhishma and Drona, who lead the earth’s rulers.

1.26.summary: Arjuna looks over the battlefield and sees his relatives—fathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, and friends—on both sides.

1.27.summary: Seeing all these loved ones, Arjuna feels deep sorrow and begins to speak his anguish.
situations: I feel overwhelming sadness seeing my family divided by conflict
I’m grieving because people I love are on opposite sides of a dispute

1.28.summary: Arjuna looks at his relatives lined up for battle and feels the weight of seeing them ready to fight.

1.29.summary: His body trembles, his mouth is dry, and his hair stands on end with fear.
situations: I’m physically shaking with anxiety before a big decision
My heart races and I feel paralyzed by fear

1.30.summary: Arjuna feels his weapon slipping, his body burning, and his mind scattered, as if he cannot even stand.
situations: I feel physically and mentally exhausted before a major challenge
My confidence crumbles when I think about a confrontation
I’m trembling and can’t focus before an important presentation

I question why I’m fighting for something that no longer matters

1.34.summary: He lists again the many relatives—teachers, fathers, sons, uncles, in‑laws—who stand in the battle.

situations: I’m terrified of being forced to hurt people I love
I refuse to compromise my values even under pressure

1.36.summary: He asks what pleasure could come from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra, saying only sin would result.

I question the true cost of harming others

1.37.summary: Arjuna argues that killing their own relatives cannot bring happiness, urging Krishna to stop the fight.

I’m seeking peace instead of conflict

1.38.summary: He observes that the enemy, driven by greed, sees no evil in destroying families or harming friends.

I’m dealing with people who justify hurting loved ones for gain

1.39.summary: Arjuna asks why they, who recognize the evil of destroying families, should not turn away from this sin.

I seek insight into how scripture reflects the underlying reality

15.2.summary: The material world is like a tree whose roots are our actions, its branches are the three qualities, and its fruits are the objects of the senses that draw us in.
situations: I feel trapped by my habits and can't see why I keep repeating them
I’m overwhelmed by the constant pull of sensory pleasures
I wonder why my actions seem to keep me stuck in the same patterns
notFor: Someone grieving a death
Someone seeking only career success without inner questioning

15.3.summary: By cutting down the rooted tree of material existence with the axe of non‑attachment, we free ourselves from its entanglement.
situations: I keep clinging to outcomes and it causes me stress
I want to let go of a relationship that no longer serves me
I’m trying to stop obsessing over social media likes
notFor: People looking for a quick fix without inner work
Those who need comfort in mourning

15.4.summary: The ultimate goal is the primeval source of all activity; once we reach it, we never have to return to the cycle of birth and death.
situations: I feel lost about the meaning of life
I’m scared of death and what comes after
I want a deeper purpose beyond daily routines
notFor: Someone seeking material wealth as the ultimate aim

15.5.summary: Those who are free from pride and attachment, who dwell in the Self and have turned away desire, transcend pleasure and pain and attain the eternal goal.
situations: I’m exhausted by constant emotional highs and lows
I struggle with pride that blocks my relationships
I want to feel lasting inner peace despite external circumstances
notFor: People looking for external validation as a solution

15.6.summary: In the supreme abode, neither sun, moon nor fire shine; those who reach it never return.
situations: I feel that ordinary comforts are insufficient for true fulfillment
I’m curious about what lies beyond physical existence
I want reassurance that there is a state beyond worldly light
notFor: Someone seeking literal physical travel to a place

15.7.summary: The divine portion that becomes a living soul draws the five senses and the mind, remaining rooted in nature.
situations: I feel my mind is scattered across many sensory cravings
I want to understand why I’m drawn to certain experiences
I seek balance between my inner self and the outer world

15.8.summary: When the soul takes on a body and later leaves it, it carries its subtle qualities just as wind carries fragrance from flowers.
situations: I’m anxious about what happens after death
I wonder why certain traits stay with me across lifetimes
I feel a sense of continuity beyond my physical form
notFor: Someone looking for a scientific explanation of genetics

15.9.summary: The mind and the senses preside over perception, enjoying whatever objects they encounter.
situations: I notice I’m constantly chasing new sensory experiences
I feel my mind is ruled by fleeting pleasures
I want to observe how my senses influence my choices

15.10.summary: The deluded cannot see the ever‑present divine who pervades all, but those with true insight perceive Him.
situations: I feel blind to deeper meaning in everyday life
I’m seeking a way to develop inner vision beyond the material
I want to move from confusion to clear understanding
notFor: People looking for a literal visual sight

15.11.summary: Yogis who strive for perfection see the divine dwelling in the Self, while the unrefined, despite effort, do not perceive Him.
situations: I practice meditation but feel I’m not progressing
I wonder why some people seem spiritually advanced while I’m stuck
I want guidance on deepening my inner practice

15.12.summary: The light that shines in the sun, moon, and fire is ultimately the Lord’s own light.
situations: I’m fascinated by the connection between the cosmos and the divine
I seek reassurance that the universe reflects a higher presence
I feel awe at natural illumination and want spiritual meaning

15.13.summary: The Lord pervades the earth, sustaining all beings with His energy, and as the moon’s water he nourishes all plants.
situations: I feel disconnected from nature and want to feel its support
I’m caring for plants and wonder about a deeper purpose
I seek to recognize the divine’s presence in everyday sustenance

15.14.summary: The Lord explains that He pervades every living being as the subtle fire that works with the vital breaths to transform the four kinds of food into nourishment.
situations: I feel disconnected from my body’s natural rhythms
I struggle to understand how my thoughts and actions affect my health
I’m curious about the spiritual aspect of digestion and metabolism

15.15.summary: He says He resides in every heart, being the source of both memory and knowledge and their loss, and that He is the ultimate truth expressed in all the Vedas.
situations: I’m searching for a deeper meaning behind my memories
I feel lost about what truly matters in life
I’m studying spiritual texts and wonder about their ultimate source

15.16.summary: There are two kinds of beings: the perishable, which includes all created forms, and the imperishable Kutastha, the unchanging reality.
situations: I’m anxious about aging and death
I feel my identity is constantly changing and want stability
I’m trying to grasp the difference between my body and my true self

15.17.summary: The Supreme Purusha, the highest Self, is an indestructible presence that sustains the three worlds.
situations: I feel overwhelmed by life’s responsibilities and need a sense of support
I’m looking for a stable foundation amid chaos
I wonder how a higher power can be present in everyday life

15.18.summary: Beyond both the perishable and the imperishable, the Lord declares Himself the supreme Purusha, the highest reality acknowledged in the Vedas.
situations: I’m seeking the ultimate truth beyond material existence
I feel my spiritual practice has plateaued and need a higher perspective
I’m studying scriptures and want to understand the highest teaching

15.19.summary: Anyone who truly understands the Lord as the highest Purusha worships Him with complete devotion of heart.
situations: I struggle to feel genuine devotion in my practice
I want to align my heart fully with my spiritual beliefs
I feel disconnected from the divine and seek a way to reconnect

15.20.summary: When this secret knowledge is realized, a person becomes wise and all of his duties are naturally fulfilled.
situations: I feel stuck in my work and doubt its purpose
I’m looking for inner wisdom to guide my daily actions
I want to perform my responsibilities without inner conflict

16.1.summary: The Lord lists divine qualities: fearlessness, pure heart, steady knowledge, yoga, charity, sense control, sacrifice, study, austerity, and honesty.
situations: I want to cultivate courage and purity in my life
I’m trying to develop a disciplined spiritual routine
I feel my actions are not aligned with my values

16.2.summary: He continues with divine traits: harmlessness, truth, lack of anger, renunciation, peace, honesty, compassion, non‑covetousness, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness.
situations: I’m dealing with frequent anger and want calmness
I struggle with jealousy and want to feel content
I aim to be more compassionate in my relationships

16.3.summary: He adds that vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, and freedom from hatred and pride belong to those destined for a divine state.
situations: I feel weak after a setback and need inner strength
I find it hard to forgive myself or others
I’m battling pride and want humility

16.4.summary: Conversely, hypocrisy, arrogance, self‑conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance characterize a demoniacal nature.
situations: I notice I’m often defensive and want to change that
I catch myself acting out of selfish pride
I feel trapped in negative patterns and need a way out

16.5.summary: Divine qualities lead to liberation, while demoniacal ones cause bondage; the Lord comforts Arjuna, reminding him of his inherent divine endowments.
situations: I feel discouraged about my spiritual progress
I worry that my flaws will keep me stuck
I need reassurance that I have innate goodness

16.6.summary: Krishna explains that there are two kinds of people: the divine, who follow righteousness, and the demoniacal, whose nature is opposite and harmful.
situations: I think I’m better than others and dismiss their feelings
I justify selfish actions because I believe I’m entitled
I feel detached from any moral standard and act only for personal gain
notFor: seeking comfort after loss
confusion about spiritual duties

16.7.summary: The demoniacal lack knowledge of what is right or wrong, and they have no purity, proper conduct, or truth in them.
situations: I’m unsure what ethical line I should not cross and keep crossing it
I act without any sense of honesty or integrity
I feel my actions are driven only by impulse, not by any moral guide
notFor: questions about divine nature

16.8.summary: They claim the universe has no truth, no moral basis, no God, and is just a product of lustful desire.
situations: I feel life is meaningless and question any higher purpose
I argue that nothing is real except personal pleasure
I’m stuck in nihilistic thinking that everything is just random
notFor: grief over a specific loss

16.9.summary: Because of this false view, such low‑intellect, fierce souls become enemies of the world, working toward its destruction.
situations: I act aggressively because I think the world owes me something
I feel my anger and selfishness are harming my community
I justify destructive behavior as a way to prove my strength
notFor: seeking peace after a conflict

16.10.summary: They are driven by endless cravings, hypocrisy, pride, arrogance, and deluded evil ideas, acting with impure motives.
situations: I notice I’m constantly craving more without satisfaction
I put on a righteous front while acting selfishly
I feel trapped by my own arrogance and cannot see my faults
notFor: questions about duty

16.11.summary: They devote themselves to endless cares that end only in death, believing that satisfying lust is the highest goal.
situations: I chase pleasure as if it’s the only purpose of life
I feel my endless worries will never end and only lead to burnout
I think that personal gratification justifies any sacrifice
notFor: grieving a loved one

16.12.summary: Bound by countless hopes, driven by lust and anger, they acquire wealth by unlawful means for sensual enjoyment.
situations: I justify cheating or fraud to get more money for fun
I’m caught in a cycle of wanting more wealth to satisfy my cravings
I let anger push me to take shortcuts that hurt others
notFor: seeking spiritual knowledge

16.13.summary: They claim ownership of whatever they acquire today and promise to keep gaining more in the future.
situations: I feel entitled to everything I own and fear losing it
I obsess over accumulating more possessions for status
I promise myself endless growth without considering the cost
notFor: coping with loss

16.14.summary: They boast of killing enemies, being powerful, perfect, and happy, seeing themselves as the ultimate lord.
situations: I brag about my achievements to feel superior
I equate power with personal worth
I think happiness comes from dominating others
notFor: seeking humility

16.15.summary: They pride themselves on noble birth, wealth, and ritual, believing these make them equal to others, yet they are deluded by ignorance.
situations: I rely on my family name or wealth to feel important
I think performing rituals makes me morally superior
I compare myself to others based on status
notFor: questions about divine nature

16.16.summary: Confused by many fantasies and trapped in delusion, they become addicted to lust and fall into a terrible hell.
situations: I feel my mind is full of endless fantasies that lead to harmful actions
I’m addicted to sensual pleasures despite knowing they harm me
I fear the consequences of my reckless desires
notFor: grief over a death

16.17.summary: They are self‑conceited, stubborn, proud of wealth, and perform ostentatious sacrifices that go against true scriptural teachings.
situations: I perform charitable acts just to show off my status
I cling to my wealth and refuse to change even when it’s harmful
I follow rituals without understanding their deeper purpose
notFor: seeking inner peace after conflict

16.18.summary: People dominated by ego, power, pride, lust and anger become hostile toward the Divine both within themselves and toward others.
situations: I keep feeling jealous and resentful when others succeed
I act aggressively to protect my status at work
I notice I hate people who disagree with my beliefs

16.19.summary: Those who are the worst of humanity are destined to be reborn in demonic wombs, a fate of suffering.
situations: I worry that my selfish actions will have lasting negative consequences
I feel trapped in a cycle of harmful behavior
I fear becoming a person I despise

16.20.summary: Being born repeatedly into demoniacal conditions, they never attain the Divine and sink even lower.
situations: I feel stuck in a pattern of self‑destructive choices
I see my life getting worse despite trying harder
I fear that my negative habits are pulling me deeper

16.21.summary: Lust, anger and greed are the three gates to this hell; abandoning them is essential.
situations: I am constantly craving more money and never feel satisfied
My anger flares and ruins relationships
I chase success but feel empty

16.22.summary: A person who frees himself from those three gates lives rightly and reaches the Supreme Goal.
situations: I want to stop being ruled by greed and find inner peace
I seek a way to live ethically without being driven by desire
I aim for spiritual growth beyond material cravings

16.23.summary: If one discards scriptural guidance and follows desire alone, he cannot achieve perfection, happiness, or the Supreme Goal.
situations: I feel lost because I ignore traditional advice and follow fleeting urges
I’m unsure whether to trust my instincts or established teachings
I’m chasing personal goals but feel unfulfilled

16.24.summary: Therefore, let the scriptures be your authority to discern right and wrong actions in this world.
situations: I need guidance on ethical decisions at work
I’m confused about what values to follow in daily life
I want a reliable source for moral choices

17.1.summary: Arjuna asks what the nature of those who perform sacrifice without scriptural guidance is—Sattva, Rajas, or Tamas?

17.2.summary: Krishna explains that faith is threefold, reflecting a person’s inherent nature: pure (Sattvic), passionate (Rajasic), or deluded (Tamasic).
situations: I wonder why my spiritual practice feels so different from others
I feel my motivations are either too calm or too restless

17.3.summary: One’s character is shaped by his faith; as his faith is, so he becomes.
situations: I want to change my habits but feel stuck in my current identity
I notice my beliefs are influencing my daily actions

17.4.summary: Pure people worship the gods, passionate people worship demi‑gods and demons, and deluded people worship ghosts and spirits.
situations: I’m confused about the objects of my devotion
I feel drawn to harmful influences despite knowing they’re negative

17.5.summary: Those who perform extreme austerities not prescribed by scripture, driven by hypocrisy, ego, lust and attachment, are misguided.
situations: I’m pushing myself into harsh practices to prove worth
I feel compelled to follow trends in spirituality that don’t feel right

17.6.summary: Krishna warns that harming the body and the divine presence within it is driven by demonic impulses.
situations: I keep overworking my body and feeling guilty about neglecting my health
I treat my own body harshly as punishment for past mistakes
I indulge in self‑destructive habits and feel stuck

17.7.summary: He explains that food, sacrifice, austerity and charity each have three qualities—pure, passionate, or inert—and we must learn to distinguish them.
situations: I’m confused about why some diets make me feel better than others
I want to understand why certain charitable acts feel hollow
I’m trying to choose a spiritual practice that feels authentic

17.8.summary: Foods that are fresh, wholesome, and pleasing promote health, happiness, and vitality for those of a pure nature.
situations: I feel sluggish and wonder if my diet is the cause
I want to eat in a way that supports my mental clarity
I’m looking for foods that boost my mood naturally

17.9.summary: Spicy, sour, salty, hot or dry foods appeal to a restless mind and can lead to pain, sorrow, and illness.
situations: I notice I crave junk food when I’m stressed and feel worse afterward
I suffer frequent digestive problems and suspect my diet
I eat for excitement rather than nourishment

17.10.summary: Rotten, impure, or stale foods attract a dull, inert nature and are harmful to body and spirit.
situations: I keep eating processed snacks that leave me feeling lethargic
I struggle with cravings for sugary drinks that give me a crash
I feel mentally foggy after meals of low‑quality food

17.11.summary: A sacrifice performed without desire for reward, out of sincere duty and faith, is pure and uplifting.
situations: I want to volunteer but worry about recognition
I feel conflicted about doing my job for a raise versus doing it well
I’m trying to practice generosity without expecting thanks

17.12.summary: Offering a sacrifice seeking fame or reward is driven by passion and leads to attachment.
situations: I work overtime hoping for a promotion rather than for the work itself
I post on social media to gain likes rather than to share genuinely
I give gifts hoping the recipient will owe me

17.13.summary: Rituals that lack scriptural guidance, distribution, chants, gifts, or faith are inert and harmful.
situations: I’m part of a group practice that feels empty and rote
I follow traditions without understanding their purpose
I feel disconnected from my spiritual community’s rituals

17.14.summary: True bodily austerities include reverence for the divine, teachers, purity, honesty, celibacy, and non‑violence.
situations: I want to adopt a healthier lifestyle that aligns with my values
I’m seeking ways to practice non‑violence in daily actions
I feel my habits conflict with my spiritual ideals

17.15.summary: Austerity of speech means speaking calmly, truthfully, pleasantly, and helpfully, and studying sacred texts.
situations: I often argue and want to communicate more peacefully
I struggle to speak truthfully when it’s uncomfortable
I want to incorporate regular study of spiritual teachings

17.16.summary: Mental austerity is calmness, kindness, self‑control, and purity of thought.
situations: I get easily agitated and want to cultivate inner calm
I notice negative thoughts spiraling and need self‑control
I aim to develop a kinder attitude toward myself and others

17.17.summary: Those who practice these three forms of austerity—body, speech, mind—with firm faith and no desire for reward are considered pure.
situations: I’m looking for a holistic approach to personal growth
I want to align my actions, words, and thoughts with my spiritual goals
I feel my efforts are motivated by selfish gain rather than sincerity

17.18.summary: Doing austerities just to gain praise, honor or worship, or to appear virtuous, is classified as Rajasic—it is unstable and driven by ego.
situations: I volunteer for a charity event just to look good on social media
I follow a strict diet hoping others will admire my discipline
I practice meditation hoping it will earn me respect
notFor: someone grieving a loss
someone seeking spiritual insight beyond ego

17.19.summary: Austerities performed out of foolishness, self‑torture, or with the intention to harm others are Tamasic—dark, harmful, and unwholesome.
situations: I push myself to the point of exhaustion thinking it's the only way to be strong
I fast aggressively to punish myself for a mistake
I engage in harsh self‑criticism hoping to change others
notFor: people looking for healthy self‑improvement
those seeking balanced discipline

17.20.summary: A gift given selflessly, at the right time, to a worthy person, as a duty without expecting anything, is Sattvic—pure and beneficial.
situations: I donate to a friend in need without expecting thanks
I help a colleague because it’s the right thing, not for a favor
I give a present to a mentor out of gratitude, not for a return
notFor: someone trying to manipulate others with gifts
someone giving out of obligation only

17.21.summary: A gift given with the hope of receiving something back, for reward, or reluctantly, is Rajasic—motivated by desire and attachment.
situations: I give a gift hoping the recipient will invite me to their party
I help a neighbor only because I expect a favor later
I donate reluctantly because I feel pressured
notFor: pure altruistic giving
mandatory charitable duties

17.22.summary: A gift offered at the wrong time, to unworthy people, or with disrespect, is Tamasic—it is inauspicious and unhelpful.
situations: I give money to someone who will misuse it
I offer praise to someone who doesn’t value it
I make a donation just to show off, but the cause is dubious
notFor: genuine charitable acts
giving to those in genuine need

17.23.summary: The mantra “Om Tat Sat” is the triple name of Brahman; from it originated the Brahmanas, the Vedas and the sacrificial rites.

17.24.summary: The utterance “Om” marks the beginning of all sacrificial acts, gifts and austerities as prescribed in the scriptures, especially for students of the divine.

17.25.summary: Reciting “Tat” without attachment to results sanctifies sacrifices, austerities and gifts performed by seekers of liberation.
situations: I practice yoga without worrying about how quickly I’ll improve
I give charity without expecting acknowledgment
I fast for spiritual growth, not for praise
notFor: someone focused on material gain from rituals

17.26.summary: ‘Sat’ denotes reality, goodness and auspicious action; it signifies what is truly beneficial and pure.
situations: I choose a career that aligns with my values
I act honestly even when lying would be easier
I support actions that promote overall well‑being
notFor: justifying harmful actions as ‘realistic’

17.27.summary: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and giving, when done for the Supreme, is called ‘Sat’; such actions are inherently pure.
situations: I volunteer regularly because it feels aligned with my deeper purpose
I maintain a simple lifestyle as an offering to something greater
I persist in my spiritual practice despite challenges
notFor: performing rituals solely for social status

17.28.summary: Any sacrifice, gift or austerity performed without faith is ‘Asat’; it has no real value now or after death.
situations: I go through a ritual feeling indifferent
I give money out of habit, not belief
I fast without any inner conviction
notFor: genuine heartfelt devotion

18.1.summary: Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the true essence of renunciation and abandonment, seeking clear guidance on these spiritual concepts.
situations: I feel confused about what it means to let go of my career ambitions
I’m unsure how to practice detachment in daily life
I’m seeking a deeper understanding of spiritual surrender
notFor: someone who already fully understands renunciation

18.2.summary: The Lord explains that true renunciation is not giving up work, but giving up the desire for its results, which wise people call Tyaga.
situations: I feel stuck doing a job I don’t enjoy because I’m attached to the salary
I keep working on projects hoping for praise rather than for the work itself
I’m afraid to start a new venture because I’m worried about the outcome

18.3.summary: Some thinkers say all actions should be abandoned as harmful, while others argue that sacrificial, charitable, and austere deeds should still be performed.
situations: I’m debating whether volunteering is a waste of time
I wonder if my religious rituals are pointless
I’m confused about whether I should stop working altogether

18.4.summary: The Lord announces that there are three kinds of abandonment, and He will now reveal the final truth about them.

18.5.summary: Acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be dropped; they cleanse the wise when performed.
situations: I feel guilty for taking a break from my spiritual practice
I wonder if charitable work is still valuable when I’m busy
I’m hesitant to donate because I think I should focus on my own needs

18.6.summary: Even these actions must be done without attachment or craving for rewards; that is the Lord’s firm conviction.
situations: I keep checking emails for compliments after a presentation
I volunteer hoping people will notice me
I work overtime hoping for a promotion rather than for the task itself

18.7.summary: Renouncing obligatory duties out of ignorance is considered a tamasic (dark) abandonment and is not proper.
situations: I want to quit my job because I’m bored, ignoring my responsibilities
I think I should avoid family duties because they’re inconvenient
I feel it’s okay to skip required chores because I don’t see their value

18.8.summary: Abandoning action out of fear of physical discomfort is a rajasic (passionate) renunciation that does not earn true merit.
situations: I avoid exercise because it hurts my muscles
I skip difficult conversations fearing awkwardness
I refuse to take on a project because I anticipate stress

18.9.summary: When one performs obligatory actions simply because they must be done, letting go of attachment and desire for reward, that renunciation is sattvic (pure).
situations: I do my chores because they’re necessary, not for praise
I fulfill my job duties without expecting a bonus
I help a friend because it’s right, not for gratitude

18.10.summary: A truly renounced person, pure and wise, is indifferent to both unpleasant and pleasant work; his doubts are cut down.
situations: I get upset when a task is boring or when it’s exciting, losing focus
I feel anxious about whether a job will be enjoyable or not
I’m torn between loving and hating a particular responsibility

18.11.summary: No embodied being can completely stop acting, but one who gives up the desire for the fruits of action is called a renunciate.
situations: I think I must stop working to be spiritual
I feel guilty for wanting any benefit from my work
I want to quit all activity to achieve peace

18.12.summary: The three types of action results—good, bad, and mixed—follow a person after death if they cling to them, but not if they renounce the fruits.
situations: I worry that my past mistakes will haunt me forever
I fear that my good deeds won’t matter after I die
I’m anxious that my mixed actions will define my legacy

18.13.summary: The Lord will now teach the five causes, according to Sankhya philosophy, that underlie all actions.

18.14.summary: The body, mind, senses, activities, and the governing deity are all parts of the fivefold make‑up of a person.
situations: I feel overwhelmed by my thoughts and physical sensations
I’m trying to understand why I react the way I do in stressful situations

18.15.summary: Every action you perform with body, speech, or mind—whether good or bad—has these five elements as its cause.
situations: I’m worried that a mistake I made will ruin my reputation
I’m debating whether to speak up at work because I fear backlash

18.16.summary: If you mistakenly think the isolated self is the doer, you are misled by an untrained mind and fail to see the true nature of the self.
situations: I blame myself completely for a project’s failure
I feel lost about who I really am beyond my roles

18.17.summary: When ego‑based thinking is gone and the mind is pure, even if you kill a living being you are not truly bound by that action.
situations: I’m haunted by a decision that caused harm to someone
I struggle with guilt after a competitive sport injury
notFor: people seeking justification for violent behavior

18.18.summary: Knowledge, the object known, and the knower together create the three‑fold impulse that drives action; the organ, the action, and the agent are its three bases.
situations: I’m trying to understand why I react emotionally in certain situations
I want to see how my thoughts, feelings, and actions are linked

18.19.summary: Sankhya teaches that knowledge, action, and actor each have three types, classified according to the three gunas.
situations: I’m studying personality types and want a spiritual framework
I feel my habits are driven by deeper qualities I can’t name

18.20.summary: Seeing the same indestructible reality in every being, without seeing them as separate, is Sattvic knowledge.
situations: I feel disconnected from others and want a sense of unity
I’m seeking a compassionate view of people who are different

18.21.summary: Viewing beings as distinct, separate entities is Rajasic knowledge.
situations: I keep comparing myself to others and feel competitive
I judge people as ‘good’ or ‘bad’ and feel restless

18.22.summary: Clinging to a single effect as the whole truth, without basis, is Tamasic knowledge.
situations: I obsess over one outcome and feel anxious when it doesn’t happen
I treat a single failure as defining my whole worth

18.23.summary: An action performed without attachment, love, hatred, or desire for reward, and in accordance with duty, is Sattvic.
situations: I want to work without fearing praise or criticism
I’m trying to serve others without expecting thanks

18.24.summary: An action driven by desire for personal gain, ego, or intense effort is Rajasic.
situations: I’m motivated only by a promotion and feel stressed
I act out of pride and become restless when results aren’t immediate

18.25.summary: An action done out of delusion, ignoring consequences, injury, or one’s ability, is Tamasic.
situations: I’m considering a risky gamble despite knowing the odds are against me
I act impulsively without thinking about how it will affect others

18.26.summary: A person who acts without attachment, ego, or craving for results, and stays steady whether they succeed or fail, is described as pure (Sattvic).
situations: I feel anxious about whether my project will be praised or criticized
I keep worrying about getting a promotion and it affects my work
I get upset when I lose a competition and feel like a failure
notFor: Someone grieving a death

18.27.summary: Someone driven by desire for reward, who is greedy, harsh, and swayed by pleasure and pain, is called passionate (Rajasic).
situations: I keep chasing bonuses even when it harms my health
I feel angry when I don’t get the recognition I think I deserve
I’m constantly comparing myself to others and feeling dissatisfied

18.28.summary: A person who is unstable, coarse, dishonest, lazy, and prone to procrastination is described as dark (Tamasic).
situations: I procrastinate and feel stuck in a cycle of guilt
I act selfishly without caring about consequences
I feel constantly exhausted and unable to start anything

18.29.summary: Krishna invites Arjuna to listen to the three kinds of intellect and resolve, each linked to a quality (Guna).

18.30.summary: The intellect that discerns right action, knows what to do and what not to do, and is free from fear, is pure (Sattvic).
situations: I’m unsure whether to speak up at work or stay silent
I feel conflicted about taking a job that pays well but feels unethical
I’m trying to decide if I should help a friend even when it’s inconvenient

18.31.summary: The intellect that misinterprets duty, confuses right and wrong, and is driven by desire, is passionate (Rajasic).
situations: I keep justifying actions that hurt others because I think they’re necessary
I feel torn between what I want and what I know is right
I rationalize selfish choices as being for the greater good

18.32.summary: The intellect clouded by darkness that sees wrongdoing as right and is perverted in understanding is dark (Tamasic).
situations: I convince myself that cheating is acceptable because everyone does it
I feel hopeless and see no difference between good and bad actions
I’m stuck in a negative mindset that labels everything as bad

18.33.summary: Steadfast resolve that, through yoga, controls the mind, breath, and senses is pure (Sattvic).
situations: I want to develop a regular meditation practice but keep getting distracted
I struggle to keep my emotions in check during stressful situations
I aim to reduce cravings for food or media

18.34.summary: When resolve is driven by attachment to duty, pleasure, or wealth, it is passionate (Rajasic).
situations: I work overtime because I fear losing my status
I chase wealth even when it harms my relationships
I feel compelled to fulfill expectations even when they cause stress

18.35.summary: A dull resolve that clings to sleep, fear, grief, despair, and arrogance belongs to the dark (Tamasic).
situations: I stay in bed to avoid facing my problems
I let fear stop me from trying new things
I feel bitter and superior because of my suffering

18.36.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna to listen about the three types of pleasure, which, when practiced, lead to the end of pain.

I find myself reacting with hatred to criticism

I cannot sit still for meditation because my mind is noisy
I am constantly over‑eating and want healthier habits

I want a spiritual anchor during a crisis
